title: Tuna salad sandwiches
skill: Fine chopping: celery, onion, pickles, herbs

move.title: Tiny bits, big crunch
move.body: Fine chopping means cutting food into small, even bits. Today you'll chop celery, green onions, pickles, and parsley into tiny pieces, stir them into tuna with a creamy dressing, and build sandwiches.

why.title: Sticks first, then across
why.body: Chopping a celery rib bit by bit takes forever, and the pieces come out every size. Cut it the long way into thin sticks first, then line the sticks up and cut across them. Every cut makes a whole row of tiny squares at once, all the same size.

why.title: Why so small
why.body: Big chunks of celery or pickle land in some bites and miss others, and they fall out of the sandwich. Tiny bits spread all through the tuna, so every bite gets a little crunch, a little sour, and a little green.

why.title: Keep the tip down
why.body: For herbs, rest the tip of the knife on the board and lift only the handle, up and down, like a seesaw. Your other hand presses flat on top of the blade, away from the edge. The tip never leaves the board, so the knife can't jump.

why.title: Squeeze out the water
why.body: Tuna and pickles both come packed in liquid. Every drop left in makes the salad runny, and runny salad soaks into the bread. Press the tuna dry and pat the pickles with a paper towel, and the sandwich holds together.

wrong.fix: Tip the bowl and spoon off the liquid, or stir in more tuna. Next time, press the can lid down hard to drain it.

wrong.sign: The celery pieces are big and uneven
wrong.fix: Line up a few more sticks and cut across again. Thinner sticks make smaller bits.
Stir in a pinch more salt and a squeeze more lemon, then taste again.

wrong.sign: The bread is soggy by lunch
wrong.fix: Put a lettuce leaf between the bread and the tuna, or pack the tuna salad separately and build the sandwich when you eat.

quiz.q: What's the fastest way to chop celery into tiny bits?
choices: Chop it into chunks and keep chopping
Cut it into thin sticks, then cut across them
quiz.explain: Each cut across a row of sticks makes many tiny squares at once.

quiz.q: Why do you press the water out of the tuna?
quiz.explain: Extra liquid makes the salad runny and soaks into the bread.

substitutions.note: Greek yogurt is a little tangier. Taste before adding the lemon juice, and use less if it's sour enough.

steps.text: Open the cans of tuna with the can opener. Hold each can over the sink and press the lid down into the can to squeeze out all the water.
steps.tip: Press with your palm flat on the middle of the lid. The edge of a cut lid is as sharp as a knife.

steps.text: Tip the tuna into the large bowl and break it into small flakes with the fork.
Rinse the celery, green onions, and parsley in the colander. Pat the parsley dry in the kitchen towel.
Cut the ends off each celery rib. Cut each rib into pieces about 3 inches long, lay them curved side up, and cut them the long way into thin sticks.
steps.tip: Hold the food with your hand shaped like a claw: fingertips tucked under, knuckles in front.

steps.text: Line up a handful of sticks side by side and chop across them into tiny squares. Add them to the bowl.
steps.look: Little green squares about the size of a pea or smaller.

steps.text: Cut the root ends and any floppy dark tops off the green onions. Line them up and slice them into very thin rings. Add them to the bowl.
Cut each pickle in half the long way, lay it flat side down, and cut it into thin sticks. Chop across the sticks into tiny bits. Pat them with a paper towel and add them to the bowl.
steps.tip: Pickles are slippery. The flat side down keeps them still.

steps.text: Push the parsley leaves into a tight pile and chop them fine: rest the tip of the knife on the board, press your other hand flat on top of the blade, and rock the handle up and down until the bits are small. Add them to the bowl.
Add the mayonnaise, mustard, lemon juice, {qty:salt} salt, and pepper. Stir with the wooden spoon until everything is coated.
steps.look: Creamy, with green flecks all through it and no dry tuna left.

steps.text: Taste a little on a clean spoon. Add a pinch more salt or a squeeze more lemon if it needs it.
steps.tip: Use a fresh spoon each time you taste, and never dip a licked spoon back in.

steps.text: Lay out half the bread. Add a lettuce leaf if you're using it, then a big scoop of tuna salad spread to the edges, then tomato slices if you're using them. Top with the rest of the bread.
steps.tip: The lettuce keeps the bread from getting soggy.

steps.text: Cut each sandwich in half from corner to corner.
steps.tip: Put any leftover tuna salad back in the fridge within 2 hours. Mayonnaise salads shouldn't sit out.

add.text: Open the cans of tuna with the can opener.
add.tip: Keep your fingers away from the lid's cut edge.

add.text: Tip the tuna into the large bowl. Break it into small flakes with the fork.
Rinse the celery, green onions, and parsley. Pat them dry with paper towels.
add.tip: Dry food doesn't slip under the knife.

add.text: Lay a damp paper towel flat under the cutting board.
add.look: Push the board gently. It shouldn't slide.

add.text: Trim the ends off the celery. Cut each rib into pieces about 3 inches long with the paring knife.
add.tip: Hold the celery with the claw grip, fingertips tucked under.

add.text: Lay each piece curved side up. Cut it the long way into thin sticks.
Line up a few sticks. Cut across them into tiny squares, and add them to the bowl.
add.look: Little green squares about the size of a pea.

add.text: Trim the roots off the green onions. Line them up and slice them into thin rings. Add them to the bowl.
Cut each pickle in half the long way. Lay the halves flat side down.
add.tip: Flat side down, a slippery pickle can't roll.

add.text: Cut the halves into thin sticks, then across into tiny bits. Pat them dry and add them to the bowl.
Set the knife down flat at the top of the board, blade facing away from you.
add.tip: Do this every time you stop cutting.

add.text: Pull the parsley leaves off the stems. Tear them into small bits over the bowl.
add.tip: Tearing herbs needs no knife, and they taste the same.

add.text: Add the mayonnaise, mustard, lemon juice, {qty:salt} salt, and pepper. Stir with the wooden spoon.
add.look: Creamy, with green flecks all through it and no dry tuna left.

add.tip: The lettuce keeps the bread from getting soggy.

add.text: Spread a big scoop of tuna salad to the edges. Add tomato slices if you're using them.
add.look: Tuna salad right to the edges of the bread.

add.text: Top with the rest of the bread. Cut each sandwich in half with the bread knife, sawing gently.
add.tip: Put leftover tuna salad in the fridge within 2 hours.
